newsitem.title: UK: India saves Gandhi papers from jaws of commerce.
newsitem.headline: India saves Gandhi papers from jaws of commerce.

text.p: A fevered dispute over the ownership of a collection of writings by Mahatma Gandhi was resolved on Friday when a Hawaii-based Hindu charity handed them over to the Indian government.
The papers, dating from the last six months of Gandhi's life, were sent to London earlier this year by the charity, the Saiva Siddhanta Church, which wanted to raise money to build a Hindu temple.
But the Indian government intervened, insisting that all of the independence leader's writings belonged to the nation.
A three-way dispute erupted between the Saiva Siddhanta Church, the Indian government and Phillips, the auction house that was appointed to sell the papers.
Eventually, the Church, which had received the papers from one of Gandhi's former secretaries, agreed to give them to India. They were handed over at the Indian High Commission (embassy) in London.

Orange-robed disciples from the Saiva Siddhanta Church, Nehru-jacketed Indian officials, besuited Phillips' representatives and photographers and reporters stood around a long mahogany table beneath a portrait of Gandhi to see the papers sealing the agreement signed.
The yellowed, postcard-sized letters in Gandhi's sprawling handwriting had been inserted into oversized albums placed in turn in brown boxes.

"When we first received the papers we did not know what we had, but when Phillips' investigations showed that they were a valuable part of India's heritage we realised they should not be sold," said Acharya Veylan Swami from the charity.
The charity had hoped to raise one million pounds ($1.68 million) from the sale. Instead it paid Phillips 15,000 pounds ($25,000) as compensation for the lost sale.
India's High Commissioner in London, L.M. Singhvi, who was instrumental in stopping the sale, was triumphant.
"This is very fulfilling for the Gandhi papers represented the heritage of the nation. The legacy of Mahatma Gandhi should not become an article of commerce," he said.

Singhvi confessed that he had become obsessed by the return of the Gandhi papers in the last few weeks, since he reportedly learned of their existence from the British press. "I was consumed to some extent by this particular issue," he said.
The papers were collected by a Gandhi acolyte, Venkataraman Kalyanam, who had kept them at his home in Madras since Gandhi was assassinated in 1948.
When Kalyanam donated them to the Saiva Siddantha Church he said he did not want any money except the price of an air ticket to visit the Hawaiian temple once it was built.
Phillips had described the papers as an outstanding insight into the mind of Gandhi, who led 350 million Indians in a non-violent campaign against British rule.

They include letters to Britain's wartime prime minister, Winston Churchill, and Louis Mountbatten, the last British viceroy of India, in which Gandhi expressed his distress at the sectarian conflicts that erupted on partition.
Fighting between Hindus and Moslems had turned Delhi into "a city of the dead", he wrote before he fasted to try to bring peace to the Indian capital.
"I had to be in Delhi to do or die...No Man, if he is pure, has anything more precious to give than his life," he said.
